issues.legal_issue: The market value in a land acquisition under a special improvement law that adopts the general acquisition procedure is determined as of the date of the special law’s preliminary notification when it serves the same function as the general law’s preliminary notification.
material_facts: The special law provided for an initial notification concerning a completed improvement scheme and a later declaration that the land was required for a public purpose.
The special law treated the later declaration as equivalent to the general acquisition law’s final declaration.
The special law contained no separate principle for determining compensation, and its general-procedure clause applied the general acquisition law so far as applicable.

The High Court used the later declaration date to determine market value, relying in part on an earlier decision interpreting a different improvement law enacted before the general acquisition law was amended.
issues.conclusion: The market value must be determined as of the special law’s initial notification, which serves the function of the general acquisition law’s preliminary notification. The appeals were allowed and the matters remanded for fresh determination on that basis.
issues.legal_principle: Under sections 27 and 16 of the City of Bangalore Improvement Act, 1945, the special notification procedure replaces the general preliminary-notification procedure where their objects and functions are identical. Section 27(2) equates the special law’s later declaration with a declaration under section 6 of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894; section 23(1) of that Act therefore supplies the market-value date, and the special initial notification corresponds to the notification under section 4(1). The words “so far as they are applicable” do not mean “only if specifically mentioned”; provisions not expressly or necessarily excluded remain applicable. Equity cannot supplant the statutory scheme, and delay between notifications does not alter the interpretation of the provisions governing the valuation date. Venkatamma v. Special Land Acquisition Officer was distinguishable because it interpreted a law enacted in 1903 against the acquisition law as it then stood; M. Manicklal v. State of Mysore was approved.

rule.if: scheme_based_land_acquisition and special_initial_notice_serves_preliminary_function and later_notice_equated_to_final_declaration and no_separate_compensation_principle

predicates.scheme_based_land_acquisition: The proceeding concerns acquisition of land under a law providing for an improvement scheme.
predicates.special_initial_notice_serves_preliminar: The special law’s initial notice performs the same preliminary function as the general acquisition procedure’s preliminary notice.
predicates.later_notice_equated_to_final_declaratio: The special law treats a later notice or declaration as equivalent to the general acquisition procedure’s final declaration.
predicates.no_separate_compensation_principle: The special law does not prescribe a distinct principle for determining compensation.

issues.definition: When an improvement-scheme acquisition uses an initial notice for the preliminary function, equates a later notice with the final declaration, and supplies no separate compensation principle, the market value is fixed at the initial notice.

issues.legal_issue: A judgment from another land valuation proceeding may be considered as additional evidence only if its relevance is established and the appellate court follows the required reasoned procedure, including allowing an opportunity to rebut it.
material_facts: The High Court admitted as additional evidence a judgment concerning other land said to be adjacent to the lands in the appeals and acquired as part of the same layout scheme.
The judgment was not between the same parties and was not a judgment in rem; an appeal against it was pending.

The acquiring authority had no opportunity to show that the other land differed in location or value, and the High Court gave no reasons demonstrating that it had considered whether admission was necessary.
issues.conclusion: The High Court’s judgment was set aside and the matters remanded. The High Court must decide, after giving the parties an opportunity to present necessary evidence, whether the other judgment may be admitted as additional evidence.
issues.legal_principle: Under section 43 of the Evidence Act, judgments outside sections 40 to 42 are irrelevant unless relevant under another provision of the Act. A judgment from another proceeding is not res judicata between different parties and is not a judgment in rem, but Khaja Fizuddin v. State of Andhra Pradesh recognizes possible relevance where it concerns similarly situated properties and valuations made on dates fairly proximate to the relevant date. Under Order 41, Rule 27 of the Code of Civil Procedure, an appellate court admitting additional evidence must be satisfied that it is required to pronounce judgment or for another substantial cause, record its reasons, and afford the opposing party an opportunity to rebut any inference from it. The Court declined to adopt an absolute exclusion of such judgments suggested in Special Land Acquisition Officer, Bombay v. Lakhamsi Ghelabhai.

rule.if: compensation_appeal and other_judgment_offered_as_additional_evidence and other_judgment_concerns_similar_property and valuation_dates_are_proximate

predicates.compensation_appeal: The proceeding is an appeal concerning compensation for acquired land.
predicates.other_judgment_offered_as_additional_evi: A party offers a judgment from a separate proceeding as additional evidence in the appeal.
predicates.other_judgment_concerns_similar_property: The separate judgment concerns property shown to be similarly situated to the property being valued.
predicates.valuation_dates_are_proximate: The valuation date addressed in the separate judgment is fairly close to the relevant valuation date in the appeal.

issues.definition: When a judgment concerning similar property and a fairly proximate valuation date is offered in a compensation appeal, its admission requires a recorded finding of necessity and an opportunity for the opposing party to rebut it.
